To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1. Nanotechnology has been applied in the field of cancer diagnosis, imaging, and therapy.

(a) metal nanoparticles can be used as contrast agents for MRI and CT imaging, as well as for photothermal therapy of tumors, and (b) the use of metal nanoparticles for these purposes is limited by their tendency to agglomerate and form aggregates in aqueous solutions.

the use of metallic nanoclusters (NCs) as imaging agents for cancer detection, and as therapeutic agents for cancer treatment, is a promising strategy for the development of novel cancer diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the design, synthesis and application of metal nanoparticles for cancer imaging, diagnosis and therapy.

the synthesis and characterization of metallic nanoclusters for use as contrast agents in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and as photothermal agents for cancer therapy.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the development of nanomaterials has been a major breakthrough for cancer imaging and therapy.
the use of nanoparticles in cancer therapy and imaging is a very promising field of research, which has already been proven by the clinical trials of some nanoparticles.
there is no single method that is superior to the others in the detection of cancer, but rather a combination of methods is required for an effective diagnosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are developing a new class of nanomaterials for biomedical applications.
we developed and evaluated the use of metal nanoclusters for imaging and therapy.
we are developing new nanotechnology based on metallic nanoclusters to image and treat cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have demonstrated the feasibility of using a novel class of nanomaterials called metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) for the delivery of a therapeutic drug to a cancer cell.
the size, shape, and surface chemistry of metallic nanoclusters can be tuned to control their optical properties and thus their ability to image and/or treat cancer cells.
the combination of a nanocluster-based contrast agent and nanocluster-mediated photodynamic therapy (PDT) can provide a synergistic therapeutic effect in the treatment of cancer.
